documents.title: Generative AI in the Classroom
documents.summary: CIPD guidance explains that unauthorized AI use falls under the Student Code of Conduct, that detectors are unreliable, and offers assignment designs that discourage AI or use it for critique and drafting. It points instructors to suggested syllabus language and consultations.
documents.stance_why: The guide sets no university-wide rule of its own; it says the academic integrity policy 'already prohibits the use of unauthorized resources, including AI content generators', then advises instructors on discouraging or integrating AI and on syllabus language, leaving classroom choices to instructors, so delegates.

units.why: The page's headline conclusion says the academic integrity policy 'already prohibits the use of unauthorized resources, including AI content generators'; this classifies unauthorized AI use as an integrity violation, so P36 (misconduct) fits better than P06 because no fallback for silent syllabi is stated.
units.anchor: academic integrity policy already prohibits the use of unauthorized resources, including AI content generators

units.why: The Center 'has updated the suggested academic integrity syllabus statement' to mention AI. This is a suggested template the center maintains, not a requirement that syllabi carry it (so not P09), and no type covers center-supplied syllabus language.
units.anchor: the Center has updated the suggested academic integrity syllabus statement to note this fact specifically
units.uncovered_note: The teaching center supplies and updates a suggested academic-integrity syllabus statement that names AI (an optional template, not a mandate).

units.why: The guide defines generative AI as 'services that use artificial intelligence to create content using natural human language', setting what the guide covers, so P61.
units.anchor: services that use artificial intelligence to create content using natural human language

units.why: Explains the integrity concern: students 'could use AI content generators to avoid producing their own work' like 'paying someone else to write a paper'. This frames AI as an outside source/ghostwriter, so P45 rather than P19 because it is an analogy, not a rule.
units.anchor: students could use AI content generators to avoid producing their own work in a very

units.why: States the rationale that AI 'removes all learning value in any assignment' when used uncritically and submitted as final product, so P41 (shortcuts practice that builds skill); the drafting/brainstorming exception is part of the same sentence.
units.anchor: it removes all learning value in any assignment

units.why: Notes services sometimes fabricate references ('hallucination'), a warning about AI output reliability; P31 (output is often wrong) fits though addressed descriptively to instructors.
units.anchor: sometimes using real references and sometimes fabricating them

units.why: Tells instructors to look at 'the conversations ongoing in your discipline' to see which AI uses are relevant: advice that instructors inform themselves before setting classroom policy, hence P63.
units.anchor: We highly recommend looking at the conversations ongoing in your discipline

units.why: States 'There is not yet a detection service that can definitively determine' whether content is AI-made: a claim detectors are unreliable, so P39.
units.anchor: There is not yet a detection service that can definitively determine whether content was produced

units.why: Offers style mismatch between sections as a sign of non-student work; this is process evidence used to identify misuse (P40), though it is a heuristic rather than a tool.
units.anchor: style mismatch between two sections of written work

units.why: Says that verifying a student's sources with Crossref and finding many unknowns may signal an AI-generated paper; evidence used to identify misuse, so P40.
units.anchor: verify a student’s sources and there are lots of unknowns, this may be a sign

units.why: Advises that if a student 'can’t explain how they arrived at a certain answer' it may show they did not do their own work; an explanation check used as evidence of misuse (P40) rather than a student rule (P30).
units.anchor: If a student can’t explain how they arrived at a certain answer

units.why: Instructors 'should never put their students’ work into' detectors or AI services without informed consent, citing privacy and IP; this is a faculty-side data protection rule, P50 (P59 is about teaching tasks, not student data).
units.anchor: instructors should never put their students’ work into services that claim to be able to

units.why: CIPD 'cannot recommend' use of AI detectors because none has been vetted by peer-reviewed study: detectors should not be relied on, P39.
units.anchor: we cannot recommend their use

units.why: Recommends connecting prompts to in-class discussion so 'requiring mention of topics or ideas specific to your class negates the value of AI-created content': an assignment redesign, P35.
units.anchor: Consider connecting your assignment prompts deeply to in-class discussions and activities

units.why: Suggests requiring more than one draft with in-class revision, a grading/assignment structure redesigned around AI (P35).
units.anchor: Require more than one draft of the same paper/assignment

units.why: Encourages primary research so work uses information not on the internet; an assignment redesign against AI, P35.
units.anchor: Encourage primary research, when possible, so that student work uses information not available on the

units.why: Suggests citation practices requiring DOIs/links and a Crossref report with the bibliography, an assignment design to expose fabricated citations: P35.
units.anchor: Consider using citation practices that require DOI numbers or links to validate resources

units.why: Suggests a reflective component 'that can only be created by students themselves': assignment redesign, P35.
units.anchor: Include a reflective component in your paper/assignment that can only be created by students themselves

units.why: Recommends writing prompts at higher Bloom's levels that 'require higher-level cognitive engagement'; assignment redesign, P35.
units.anchor: Develop writing prompts and other assignments at levels of Bloom’s Taxonomy that require higher-level cognitive

units.why: Suggests small assignments 'written during class time' via Canvas quiz or Nearpod, shifting weight to in-class, unassisted work: P33.
units.anchor: to allow them to be written during class time

units.why: Suggests multi-modal project types (presentations, videos, podcasts) as AI-resistant assignment design: P35.
units.anchor: Consider multi-modal project types, such as presentations, videos, or podcasts

units.why: Says group and client-based projects and problem-based learning 'are too complex for AI content generators', recommending them as assignment designs: P35.
units.anchor: Problem-based learning and design thinking are processes that are too complex for AI content generators

units.why: Suggests using AI-generated content 'for student critique and discussion', teaching students to evaluate AI output: P44 (courses demonstrate AI use) fits better than P35 as AI is used as course material.
units.anchor: Use content generated by an AI content generation service for student critique and discussion

units.why: Suggests letting students bring an AI-generated first draft to 'correct, expand, and improve'; an instructor-sanctioned use of AI in the work, P44 (P16 concerns students' own submission conditions).
units.anchor: Use content generated by an AI content generation service as a “first draft” for students

units.why: Encourages students to use AI in active-learning exercises (learn a topic with AI, then fact-check it): P44 teaching with AI, and the fact-checking element is part of the same sentence.
units.anchor: Encourage students to use an AI content generation service as a part of active learning

units.why: Proposes using AI generation 'to spark classroom discussion' so students see why to avoid it; a classroom activity redesign, P35.
units.anchor: Using AI content generation to spark classroom discussion could help students understand why they should

units.why: Says the Student Code of Conduct provisions apply to 'unauthorized use of any resource or service not authorized by or acknowledged to the instructor', which covers AI: unauthorized AI use classified as misconduct, P36.
units.anchor: unauthorized use of any resource or service not authorized by or acknowledged to the instructor

units.why: States using AI 'to solve equations or develop code' are 'unauthorized uses of assistance'; this bans AI-made solutions/code unless authorized, P19 (the submitted work is AI made), restrict because authorization can lift it.
units.anchor: Using AI content generation services to solve equations or develop code would be examples of

units.why: Says AI text in a written assignment is plagiarism 'if that content were not cited as being AI-generated'; undisclosed use is the violation, so P28 (rather than P24, which would require disclosure outright).
units.anchor: would be plagiarism if that content were not cited as being AI-generated content

units.why: Tells instructors to 'follow the same process you would during any other academic integrity concern', via Student Conduct: AI suspicions go through the ordinary integrity process, P36.
units.anchor: you should follow the same process you would during any other academic integrity concern

units.why: Says the suggested academic integrity language 'can be added to your course syllabus and discussed with your students'; an optional (may) syllabus communication, P09 as nearest fit, though it does not require a statement.
units.anchor: This language can be added to your course syllabus and discussed with your students

units.why: Offers a consultation with the Scholarly Teaching team for help incorporating suggestions: support for faculty learning to teach with AI, P63.
units.anchor: Email ProDev@ilstu.edu to set up a consultation with a member of the Center's Scholarly Teaching

documents.title: Ethical Use of Generative AI (thesis, dissertation, capstone, comprehensive exams)
documents.summary: Graduate School statement on generative AI in culminating work. It requires disclosure to the committee and citation, ties unauthorized use to Policy 1.8, and lets units add rules.
documents.stance_why: AI use in theses, dissertations, capstones and comprehensive exams is allowed 'within appropriate guidelines' but 'All use ... must be disclosed' and cited, so permit with conditions.

units.why: Says generative AI 'can support innovative and creative scholarship when used within appropriate guidelines, which may vary by discipline': a conditional permission for thesis work, P62 (research/scholarship), not P02 since it is not a general default.
units.anchor: can support innovative and creative scholarship when used within appropriate guidelines

units.why: Says 'transparency around the usage of generative AI is required' toward committee, department and audience: a disclosure rule, P24.
units.anchor: transparency around the usage of generative AI is required between the student, their committee and

units.why: Students must take responsibility for their work 'including using their own words and proper citations': ownership of submitted work, P29.
units.anchor: Students need to take responsibility for their work, including using their own words and proper

units.why: 'All use of generative AI ... must be disclosed to the student’s committee by the student' is a specific disclosure duty for each use, P24.
units.anchor: All use of generative AI in the thesis/dissertation/capstone/comprehensive exam process must be disclosed

units.why: Use must be 'verified to be within the standards of the discipline and school/department' by student and committee: a research-governance check, P62.
units.anchor: Generative AI use should be verified to be within the standards of the discipline

units.why: 'Unauthorized use of generative AI may be considered a violation of Policy 1.8 Integrity in Research': improper use classed as misconduct, P36.
units.anchor: Unauthorized use of generative AI may be considered a violation of Policy 1.8

units.why: 'Usage of generative AI must be appropriately cited following the guidelines of the style manual': a citation duty, P24 (does not require tool/prompt detail, so not P25).
units.anchor: Usage of generative AI must be appropriately cited following the guidelines of the style manual

units.why: States 'individual schools/departments may have additional policies, guidance, or restrictions', leaving further rules to units: delegation, P04.
units.anchor: individual schools/departments may have additional policies, guidance, or restrictions

units.why: Says it is the student's responsibility to understand the standards and contact the school or Graduate School with questions: ask when unsure, P10.
units.anchor: contact their school/department or the Graduate School with any questions or concerns

units.why: Says 'additional or more detailed guidance may be issued in the future' because AI is new and evolving: provisional policy, P54.
units.anchor: additional or more detailed guidance may be issued in the future

documents.title: Artificial Intelligence (AI) at ISU
documents.summary: IT help page listing campus AI tools and a ban on entering restricted data into Copilot, plus pointers to the responsible-AI committee and evolving standards. Little teaching policy.
documents.stance_why: The page sets no teaching-and-learning stance; it lists available tools and data-handling cautions ('Do not enter ... restricted ... data into Copilot'), so it sets no stance on student AI use.

units.why: States the university 'has decided to make available several AI services on campus' (Firefly, Copilot, Zoom AI, Otter.ai): university-provided sanctioned tools, P17.
units.anchor: the University has decided to make available several AI services on campus

units.why: Says the university is 'working to develop a vision' and 'continuing to develop standards and practices' for AI: the policy is still evolving, P54.
units.anchor: The University is continuing to develop standards and practices around the use of AI at

units.why: Says it is 'strongly recommended' to read the university's vision, guidance and policies before using AI tools; a pointer to the institution-level framework, P56.
units.anchor: it is strongly recommended you familiarize yourself with the vision, guidance, and policies regarding AI

units.why: Says the Committee for the Responsible Use of AI oversees and supports standards and practices: institution-level governance structure, P56.
units.anchor: This is overseen and supported by the Committee

units.why: Tells users it is 'important to understand what can and cannot be entered' by data classification: a data-protection rule, P50.
units.anchor: it is important to understand what can and cannot be entered based on data classification

units.why: Forbids entering restricted or highly restricted data (FERPA records, PII) into Copilot, a licensed tool: personal data protection, P50.
units.anchor: Do not enter or upload any restricted or highly restricted university data into Copilot

notes: Coder B. Computing/school none found; course deferred. The IT page is partial quality with few teaching policies. P09 used for CIPD optional syllabus language is a loose fit; the suggested-syllabus-template idea is logged as UNCOVERED.
